\chapter{Name a Verb, Find Its Stem}
\label{ch:fa-core-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{6}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name five core Persian verbs in their dictionary form, recognise the -tan/-dan ending that marks any Persian infinitive, and give the present stem that each verb carries beside it.}

The five pairs run back to back from memory — budan, raftan/rav-, âmadan/â-, goftan/gu-, dânestan/dân- — with the infinitive ending named and the stem produced for each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[budan]{\fa{بودن} — “to be,” and the ending every Persian verb wears}

\label{lesson:FA-C06-budan}



\begin{quote}
Chapter 4 ended on \textbf{\fa{خوبم}} \emph{khubam}, “I am well.” That \textbf{-am} carried “I am” with no verb beside it. This chapter names the verb it belongs to.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one verb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{بودن}} — \emph{budan} — \textbf{to be}
\end{quote}

Four letters, all of them already yours. From the right edge: \textbf{\fa{ب}} \emph{b}, \textbf{\fa{و}} long \emph{u}, \textbf{\fa{د}} \emph{d}, \textbf{\fa{ن}} \emph{n}. Persian \textbf{\fa{و}} never joins to the letter on its left, so the word falls into two clumps, \textbf{\fa{بو}} and \textbf{\fa{دن}} — the same kind of break \textbf{\fa{ا}} makes inside \textbf{\fa{سلام}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: how a Persian verb announces itself}]
English names a verb with a word in front of it: \emph{to be}, \emph{to go}, \emph{to know}. Persian names it with an ending on the back. Every Persian infinitive — every one, with no list of exceptions — finishes in \textbf{-\fa{تن}} \emph{-tan} or \textbf{-\fa{دن}} \emph{-dan}.

\textbf{\fa{بودن}} is \emph{bu} + \emph{dan}. Whenever a Persian word ends in \emph{-tan} or \emph{-dan}, you are holding a verb in its naming form.

Persian rewards you here: one set of personal endings serves every verb. What it asks instead is one extra fact per verb — the next lesson is about that fact.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{budan} continues Middle Persian \emph{būdan}, from the Indo-European root *\emph{bheu-}, “to grow, to become, to be.” English \textbf{be} and \textbf{been} are that root, worn smooth. So are German \emph{bin}, Latin \emph{fuī} “I was” — the ancestor of English \textbf{future} — and Sanskrit \emph{bhavati}.

The resemblance runs through Persian's plainest words: \textbf{\fa{مادر}} \emph{mâdar} is \textbf{mother}, \textbf{\fa{پدر}} \emph{pedar} is \textbf{father}, \textbf{\fa{برادر}} \emph{barâdar} is \textbf{brother}, \textbf{\fa{دختر}} \emph{dokhtar} is \textbf{daughter}, \textbf{\fa{نام}} \emph{nâm} is \textbf{name}. Nobody borrowed these; both languages inherited them.

One caution to carry through the chapter: lookalikes lie. Persian \textbf{\fa{بد}} \emph{bad} does mean “bad,” but its history and the English word's are unconnected. A cousin has to be traced, not guessed.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{budan} — to be
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\fa{بودن}} from the right edge, in its two clumps
  \item \emph{Name:} the ending that marks a Persian infinitive — \textbf{-tan / -dan}
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{budan} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{bheu-} $\to$ English \textbf{be}, \textbf{been}
  \item \emph{Retrieve:} the ending on \textbf{\fa{خوبم}} that already meant “I am”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does a Persian verb announce that it is a verb? (It ends in \emph{-tan} or \emph{-dan}.) Which English word is \textbf{budan}? (\textbf{Be} — the same inherited root.) Is Persian \textbf{bad} a cousin of English \emph{bad}? (No; that one is coincidence.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%A8\%D9\%88\%D8\%AF\%D9\%86}{Wiktionary: \fa{بودن}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[raftan]{\fa{رفتن} — “to go,” and the second form that travels with it}

\label{lesson:FA-C06-raftan}



\begin{quote}
Retrieve the Persian for “to be,” and the ending that marked it as a verb. That ending returns here, on a word that brings the extra fact Persian asks of you.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one verb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{رفتن}} — \emph{raftan} — \textbf{to go}
\end{quote}

From the right edge: \textbf{\fa{ر}} \emph{r}, \textbf{\fa{ف}} \emph{f}, \textbf{\fa{ت}} \emph{t}, \textbf{\fa{ن}} \emph{n} — all four familiar, \textbf{\fa{ر}} from \textbf{\fa{چطور}} \emph{chetor} and \textbf{\fa{ف}} from \textbf{\fa{حافظ}} \emph{hâfez}. \textbf{\fa{ر}} does not join leftward, so it stands alone and \textbf{\fa{فتن}} follows as one run. The ending is the \emph{-tan} you met on \textbf{\fa{بودن}}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the second fact every Persian verb carries}]
Persian keeps two forms for each verb, and you learn them as a pair.

The first is the infinitive, \textbf{\fa{رفتن}} \emph{raftan}. Strip its \emph{-an} and you have \textbf{\fa{رفت}} \emph{raft}, the \textbf{past stem}; everything about yesterday is built on that.

The second is the \textbf{present stem}, and it cannot be predicted from the infinitive. For \emph{raftan} it is \textbf{\fa{رو}} \emph{rav}. Everything about now is built on \emph{rav-}: \emph{mi-ravam} “I go,” \emph{mi-ravad} “she goes.”

So the fact to store is not \emph{raftan} alone but \textbf{raftan $\to$ rav-}, said in one breath. Get the pair and the whole verb opens: the endings that follow a stem are the same for every Persian verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\fa{رفتن}} \emph{raftan} continues Middle Persian \emph{raftan}; its deeper Indo-European ancestry is genuinely unsettled, so no English cousin is claimed for it here.

The split itself needs no excuse — English does the same thing. \emph{Go} and \emph{went} are two unrelated words sharing one verb; so are \emph{be} and \emph{was}. English calls that irregularity and buries it in a list. Persian makes it the ordinary shape of a verb and says so up front.

\textbf{\fa{رو}} \emph{rav} is short: \textbf{\fa{ر}}, then \textbf{\fa{و}}, with no join between them. Say the pair aloud until it sounds like one item — \emph{raftan, rav}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{raftan} — to go
  \item \emph{Say it:} the pair as one item — \textbf{raftan, rav}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\fa{رفتن}}, then \textbf{\fa{رو}}
  \item \emph{Name:} the ending that made \textbf{raftan} an infinitive
  \item \emph{Retrieve:} the Chapter 6 verb meaning “to be” — \textbf{budan}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two facts does a Persian verb ask you to store? (The infinitive and its present stem.) What is the pair for “to go”? (\textbf{Raftan, rav}.) Could \emph{rav-} have been worked out from \emph{raftan}? (No — which is why it is learned with the word.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%B1\%D9\%81\%D8\%AA\%D9\%86}{Wiktionary: \fa{رفتن}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[âmadan]{\fa{آمدن} — “to come,” and an alef that wears a hat}

\label{lesson:FA-C06-amadan}



\begin{quote}
Say the pair for “to go” as one item. Now expect the same two-part shape from every verb that follows, including this one, which travels in the opposite direction.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one verb and one new shape}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{آمدن}} — \emph{âmadan} — \textbf{to come}
\end{quote}

The last three letters are old friends: \textbf{\fa{م}} \emph{m}, \textbf{\fa{د}} \emph{d}, \textbf{\fa{ن}} \emph{n}, and the \emph{-dan} ending tells you at once that this is an infinitive. The first shape is new. \textbf{\fa{آ}} is plain \textbf{\fa{ا}} with a small wavy stroke over it, called \emph{madde}, and it is what Persian writes when a word opens on long \textbf{â}. Plain \textbf{\fa{ا}} at the start of a word carries a short vowel — that is the \textbf{\fa{ا}} in \textbf{\fa{اسم}} \emph{esm}. The hat is the difference between \emph{esm} and \emph{âmadan}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{âmadan} was built from a prefix \textbf{â-}, “toward,” and the very old verb root *\emph{gwem-}, “to go, to come.” In Old Iranian that gave a form like *\emph{â-gmata-}, “come toward”; the \emph{g} wore away, the \emph{m} survived, and Middle Persian \textbf{âmad} is what was left.

That root is one of the family's great travellers. English kept it almost bare as \textbf{come}. Latin turned it into \emph{venīre}, which English then borrowed back dozens of times over: \textbf{advent}, \textbf{adventure}, \textbf{convene}, \textbf{convenient}, \textbf{event}, \textbf{invent}, \textbf{avenue}, \textbf{revenue}, \textbf{prevent}, \textbf{souvenir}. Sanskrit has \emph{gacchati}, “goes.” So \emph{âmadan} and \emph{come} are not lookalikes; they are the same word, four thousand years apart.

The present stem is \textbf{\fa{آ}} \emph{â} — a single letter — heard as \emph{ây-} before an ending: \emph{mi-âyam} “I come.” Store the pair as \textbf{âmadan, â-}. It comes from a different ancient root than the infinitive does, which is exactly why the two look nothing alike.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{âmadan} — to come
  \item \emph{Say it:} the pair as one item — \textbf{âmadan, â-}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\fa{آمدن}}, starting at the hatted alef
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{âmadan} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{gwem-} $\to$ English \textbf{come}, \textbf{advent}, \textbf{event}
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \textbf{raftan, rav-} going out; \textbf{âmadan, â-} coming in
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the little hat on \textbf{\fa{آ}} tell you? (The word opens on long \textbf{â}.) Which everyday English verb shares \emph{âmadan}'s root? (\textbf{Come}.) And what is the pair for “to come”? (\textbf{Âmadan, â-}.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%A2\%D9\%85\%D8\%AF\%D9\%86}{Wiktionary: \fa{آمدن}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[goftan]{\fa{گفتن} — “to say,” written with a letter Arabic does not have}

\label{lesson:FA-C06-goftan}



\begin{quote}
Say the pair for “to come.” Then hold the shape in mind: a name, and a present stem that has to be learned beside it. Here is a third verb built the same way.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one verb and one new letter}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{گفتن}} — \emph{goftan} — \textbf{to say, to tell}
\end{quote}

Read from the right. The last three, \textbf{\fa{ف}} \emph{f}, \textbf{\fa{ت}} \emph{t}, \textbf{\fa{ن}} \emph{n}, close the word with the familiar \emph{-tan}. The opening shape is \textbf{\fa{گ}} \emph{g}, called \emph{gâf}: a long slanting stroke with a second slanting stroke laid above it.

Arabic has no \emph{g}, so Persian made one. Persian adds four letters to the inherited Arabic set — \textbf{\fa{پ}} \emph{p}, \textbf{\fa{چ}} \emph{ch}, \textbf{\fa{ژ}} \emph{zh}, and \textbf{\fa{گ}} \emph{g} — and you have already read one of them, the \textbf{\fa{چ}} inside \textbf{\fa{چیست}} \emph{chist}. Each is an Arabic letter with extra strokes: \textbf{\fa{گ}} is the \emph{k} shape wearing a second bar.

\begin{cousinweb}
The present stem is \textbf{\fa{گو}} \emph{gu}: \textbf{\fa{گ}} then \textbf{\fa{و}}, no join between them. \emph{Mi-guyam} is “I say.” Store the pair as \textbf{goftan, gu-}.

Now the part that makes the pair unforgettable. Persian has an ordinary, everyday word for “conversation”: \textbf{\fa{گفتگو}} \emph{goftogu}. Pull it apart and it is the past stem \textbf{\fa{گفت}} \emph{goft}, a linking \emph{-o-} meaning “and,” and the present stem \textbf{\fa{گو}} \emph{gu}. A conversation is literally \emph{said-and-say}. The two halves of the verb, sitting next to each other in a noun you can hear on any Iranian news broadcast.

The verb is old. Old Persian, the language of Darius's cliff inscriptions, already had the root \emph{gaub-}, “to say, to call oneself.” Outside the Iranian branch its relatives are not securely established, so no English cousin is claimed here — and English \emph{gab} and \emph{gossip}, which look tempting, come from somewhere else entirely.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{goftan} — to say
  \item \emph{Say it:} the pair as one item — \textbf{goftan, gu-}
  \item \emph{Read it:} \textbf{\fa{گ}}, then \textbf{\fa{گو}}, then \textbf{\fa{گفتن}}
  \item \emph{Build:} \textbf{goft} + \emph{-o-} + \textbf{gu} $\to$ \textbf{goftogu}, conversation
  \item \emph{Retrieve:} the pair for “to come” — \textbf{âmadan, â-}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which letter opens \textbf{\fa{گفتن}}, and why is it not in Arabic? (\textbf{\fa{گ}} \emph{gâf}; Arabic has no \emph{g} sound.) What two pieces of the verb hide inside \textbf{goftogu}? (The past stem \emph{goft} and the present stem \emph{gu}.) Say the pair. (\textbf{Goftan, gu-}.)

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%DA\%AF\%D9\%81\%D8\%AA\%D9\%86}{Wiktionary: \fa{گفتن}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dânestan]{\fa{دانستن} — “to know,” and five pairs held together}

\label{lesson:FA-C06-danestan}



\begin{quote}
Name the ending that marks a Persian infinitive. The last verb of the chapter wears it, and every letter in the word is one you can already read.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know first — one verb and its stem}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\fa{دانستن}} — \emph{dânestan} — \textbf{to know}
\end{quote}

From the right: \textbf{\fa{د}} \emph{d}, \textbf{\fa{ا}} long \emph{â}, \textbf{\fa{ن}} \emph{n}, \textbf{\fa{س}} \emph{s}, \textbf{\fa{ت}} \emph{t}, \textbf{\fa{ن}} \emph{n}. Nothing new to decode, which is a good place to be six lessons into a script.

The present stem is \textbf{\fa{دان}} \emph{dân}: \emph{mi-dânam}, “I know.” The pair is \textbf{dânestan, dân-} — and this stem is one you can watch working. \textbf{\fa{دانش}} \emph{dânesh} is “knowledge”; add \textbf{\fa{گاه}} \emph{gâh}, “place,” and you get \textbf{\fa{دانشگاه}} \emph{dâneshgâh}, \textbf{university} — a knowledge-place, built straight off the stem.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{dânestan} belongs to the Indo-European root *\emph{gnō-}, “to know.” English inherited it three times over: \textbf{know}, and also \textbf{can} (originally “to know how”), \textbf{ken}, \textbf{cunning}, and \textbf{uncouth}, which is literally “un-known.” Latin's \emph{nōscere} sent English \textbf{notice}, \textbf{notion}, \textbf{note}, \textbf{recognise}, \textbf{cognition}, and \textbf{noble} — a noble person being a known one. Greek \emph{gnōsis} gives \textbf{diagnosis}, \textbf{prognosis}, \textbf{agnostic}. Sanskrit has \emph{jânâti}, “knows.”

One honest footnote: specialists still argue about how this root arrived in Persian wearing a \textbf{d}, when its Iranian relatives usually show a \emph{z} or \emph{zh}. The membership in the family is standard; the road it took is disputed, and this book flags that rather than smoothing it over.

Persian's other “know” is \textbf{\fa{شناختن}} \emph{shenâkhtan}, used for knowing a person rather than a fact. Its stem \textbf{\fa{شناس}} \emph{shenâs-} shows the same root more plainly — it is the \emph{gnos-} of \emph{gnosis}, wearing Iranian clothes.

And \textbf{\fa{بودن}} \emph{budan} has a present stem too: \textbf{\fa{باش}} \emph{bâsh-}. It waits for the chapter where the present tense arrives.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{dânestan, dân-} — to know
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{raftan, rav-} — to go
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{âmadan, â-} — to come
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{goftan, gu-} — to say
  \item \emph{Say it:} \textbf{budan} — to be
  \item \emph{Build:} \textbf{dân} $\to$ \textbf{dânesh} $\to$ \textbf{dâneshgâh}, university
  \item \emph{Connect:} \textbf{dânestan} $\leftarrow$ *\emph{gnō-} $\to$ English \textbf{know}, \textbf{can}, \textbf{diagnosis}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two things does a Persian verb ask you to store? (Its name in \emph{-tan} or \emph{-dan}, and its present stem.) Which English words share \textbf{dânestan}'s root? (\textbf{Know}, \textbf{can}, and the \emph{gnosis} family.) Now run all five pairs once, out loud, without the page.

Source: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%D8\%AF\%D8\%A7\%D9\%86\%D8\%B3\%D8\%AA\%D9\%86}{Wiktionary: \fa{دانستن}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
